results.summary: This 4-bit ALU performs arithmetic, logical, shift, and comparison operations on two 4-bit inputs selected by a 4-bit control signal. It provides four status flags: carry, zero, negative, and overflow. The design is intended as a basic CPU building block or teaching demo. Testing requires toggle switches for inputs and control, and LEDs for outputs and flags.

The Digital OTA is an analog operational transconductance amplifier with high output impedance. It has three analog pins: Vo (output), VA, and VB (inputs). The documentation is minimal, indicating only that it amplifies transconductance and can be tested with a function generator. No other usage details are provided.

This design drives an external ADG732 32-channel multiplexer, cycling through output channels at 1 Hz to test multistrand cables. It divides a 10 MHz clock to 1 Hz and generates chip select and write signals for the multiplexer. Testing can be done with an FPGA (e.g., iCE40) or with the actual ADG732 chip on a custom PCB. The project originated as a cable assembly test tool.

This is a two-stage CMOS operational amplifier with Miller compensation. It requires an 8 µA bias current and a 1.8 V DC supply. The differential inputs are V+ and V-, and the output is Vout. The documentation is very brief, providing only basic operating conditions.

This is a 2.4 GHz integer-N PLL with an output divide-by-100, producing a frequency range of 19.2–25.2 MHz. It uses a 20 MHz reference clock and allows digital control of the divider factor and VCO discrete tuning to overcome process variation. Outputs include an analog pin (FOUT) and two digital pins, with an analog control voltage pin (VCON) for observation. The design is analog and requires an external 20 MHz clock.

This design implements an AXI4-Lite master and slave with a simplified interface for testing memory-mapped transactions. It allows the user to initiate read and write operations using simple input signals and provides a done flag on completion. Testbenches are provided to verify functionality. The module hides the complexity of the full AXI4-Lite protocol.

This is a 16-bit bit-serial CPU with an 8-bit instruction input and 8 LED outputs. The documentation is very brief, providing only pin names and no details on the instruction set or operation. It appears to be a simple processor for educational purposes.

This project is a generative silicon art piece depicting a cross-stitch creature on the met4 layer. It has no functional pins other than a dummy output and requires no external hardware. It is purely decorative and has no test procedure.
